findings.claim: #207 changed the end-of-file branch so that what decides is the table's own rows (HighestNumber), not the index's count. The MaxXRefSectionLength branch two lines below still decides by `_xref.Count > 0`. So a table the guard cuts before its first row is kept, as the guard's, only when a newer section indexed something. Otherwise it is Malformed and the chain indexes nothing. Two consequences. (1) The whole file is rebuilt at opening and read past the guard, with xref.rebuilt (Repair) on a sound file, while a looser guard reads less. (2) The #264 judgment of the cut table's /Prev depends on what another section indexed.

checked_and_sound: Refused ranges are merged correctly. RefuseRanges joins every range that meets the last merged one in a single pass over the kept and new ranges, both sorted, and RefusedToOlderRows searches by halves over disjoint sorted ranges. Ranges are never empty: RefuseDeclared skips counts of 0, and LoseRows always passes first < end.

The refusal is bounded (invariant 4). Each refusal sorts the section's own ranges, then merges with at most 4,096 kept ones; past that every number is refused and later refusals return at once. A chain is at most MaxXRefSectionCount (1,024) sections. `_rowsLost` holds at most 4,096 entries per pass and is emptied at each window pass.

Pool rentals go back on every path. RefuseDeclared returns `declared` in a finally block. Nothing can throw between Rent and the store in RefuseRanges. Initialize's finally calls ReleaseRefusedRanges and nulls `_rowsLost` and `_refusedNumbers`, under ThrowOnLimit or a source failure too. Rent(0) yields Array.Empty, which SharedArrayPool.Return drops harmlessly (its bucket index is out of range). HostileInputTests.A_refusal_gives_back_the_arrays_it_merges_ranges_in would fail if the merged 4,096-element array were kept (+64 KB against a 96 KB margin).

No number the section did give is refused. RefuseRowsLost runs after the section's rows are indexed (ReportSectionReadInPart follows the read), so the section's own later subsections stand (ZzP3, and the batch's own test). Refusal never applies to rows read before it.

findings.claim: B19-7 lets a comment sit between a header's tokens, and that comment can hold `endobj`. The search's reads are not all the same: one that comes before the read finding the header cannot yet know where the header starts. In such a read, `StreamEnds.HoldsEndObj(span, span.Length)` and `EndObjTail.Read(..., position + span.Length)` take in the bytes past the header's start, including that comment's `endobj`. Later, once the header's start lies in an earlier read, `HoldsEndObj(span, header - position)` and `tail.Read(..., until: header)` cannot take those bytes back. Two results then change: `EndObjTail` overwrites `_keywordEnd` with the comment's keyword, so `DataEnd(header)` returns -1 and the object's own `endobj` no longer ends the data; and `endObjSeen` turns true. So the data served for a stream, its report, and whether its `endobj` is judged missing all depend on where the reads split the data. That split moves with the file's layout against the 8 KB window, and with a `MaxObjectLength` the object never reaches. EndObjTail's remark is now false: "What lies between is the header's runs of digits and white space, which make no keyword". So is the threat model's "where the reads start changes nothing". On main the comment made no header, and the outcome did not depend on the window.

findings.fix: Do not let the bytes from a possible header's start reach EndObjTail or HoldsEndObj until a read decides whether that header is one.
